name: Levothyroxine (T4)

lead: Levothyroxine is synthetic T4, the standard replacement therapy for hypothyroidism, also used to suppress TSH in some thyroid cancers. Some users with low-normal or borderline thyroid levels aim to correct them to feel better, hold less water and fat, and look leaner.

It is converted to T3, which binds thyroid hormone receptors and regulates gene transcription and metabolism. For people with low thyroid function, correcting it normalizes metabolism and energy. No trials have examined it as an appearance treatment in people with normal thyroid function.

paras: It is taken as a daily prescription tablet, with dosing guided by thyroid blood tests. On forums it is discussed mainly by people who suspect or have borderline thyroid abnormalities, sometimes alongside growth hormone.

Overdose causes hyperthyroid symptoms including arrhythmia and bone loss. The US label has a boxed warning against use for obesity or weight loss, stating that normal replacement doses are ineffective for weight reduction in euthyroid patients and larger doses may cause serious toxicity. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Some users aim to correct low-normal thyroid levels with levothyroxine to normalize metabolism and energy, hold less water and fat, and look leaner. It is the standard treatment for hypothyroidism.

lead: Levothyroxine is a synthetic form of thyroxine (T4), the main hormone made by the thyroid gland. It is the standard replacement therapy for hypothyroidism and is also used to suppress TSH in some thyroid cancers.[1][2][3]

Because excess thyroid hormone causes weight loss, levothyroxine has been misused for slimming. The US label carries a boxed warning that it should not be used to treat obesity or for weight loss, stating that doses within normal replacement ranges are ineffective for weight reduction in euthyroid patients and larger doses may cause serious toxicity.[3]

On looksmaxxing forums it is discussed mainly by people who suspect or have borderline thyroid abnormalities, sometimes alongside growth hormone. No trials have examined it as an appearance treatment in people with normal thyroid function.

paras: Levothyroxine treats primary, secondary and tertiary hypothyroidism, including congenital forms, and is used for TSH suppression in differentiated thyroid cancer.[3][2][4] Guidelines from the American Thyroid Association address its dosing and the dissatisfaction some patients report on monotherapy.[5] Treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism is debated.[6][4]

Adverse reactions are mainly those of overtreatment: weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating, anxiety, insomnia, tremor, palpitations and arrhythmias. Long-term TSH suppression has been linked to cardiac problems and reduced bone density, and it is contraindicated in thyrotoxicosis, acute myocardial infarction and uncorrected adrenal insufficiency.[3][4]

T4 is converted in peripheral tissues to the more active T3, which binds nuclear receptors and regulates gene transcription. About 80% of T3 comes from T4 deiodination.[3] Oral absorption is 40 to 80% and is reduced by calcium, iron and fibre.[4]

Thyroxine was isolated at the Mayo Clinic in 1914 and synthesised in 1927 by Harington and Barger.[4] Synthetic levothyroxine came into US clinical practice in the late 1940s and gradually replaced thyroid extracts.[1]

Forum posts show users discussing self-prescribing levothyroxine when their own bloodwork shows high-normal TSH, sometimes in combination with growth hormone.[7] Other threads mix claims about its effects on height, weight and appearance with the view of other users that it will not change looks in people without hypothyroidism.

Trials of levothyroxine concern hypothyroidism, congenital hypothyroidism, pregnancy and thyroid cancer, and bioequivalence of formulations; guidelines and reviews summarise them.[5][6] Studies in euthyroid people for cosmetic purposes were not found. The label states that euthyroid patients do not lose weight on replacement doses.[3]

lore.intro: Levothyroxine is discussed on looksmaxxing forums mainly in relation to thyroid bloodwork and hormone optimisation stacks.[7]
